extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, petitioners, counsel, and practitioners participating in AIA trials/IPR/CBM/PGR proceedings before the USPTO/PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for handling discovery, real party-in-interest/privity issues, joinder, stays, consolidation, and coordination of multiple proceedings (AIA trials, reexaminations, reissue) before the USPTO/PTAB. Focused on procedural and evidentiary principles used to manage and evaluate such proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery on secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office declines to make additional discovery on secondary considerations available as a matter of right; all other types of additional discovery may be obtained only upon a showing based on the Garmin factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing fairness with statutory deadlines, the Office will not grant automatic additional discovery for secondary considerations; requests for additional discovery must meet the Garmin-factor showing and are evaluated case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for real party-in-interest (RPI)/privity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may raise a challenge regarding a real party-in-interest or privity at any time during a trial proceeding, though the Office recognizes it is important to resolve such issues as early as possible (preferably prior to institution or in the preliminary response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early raising of RPI/privity challenges is preferred to avoid delay and cost. For late challenges that reasonably could have been raised earlier, the Office will consider the impact of delay (including whether delay is unwarranted or prejudicial) and may consider that impact when deciding whether to grant a motion for additional discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory disclosure of sensitive RPI/privity documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will not require the parties to provide highly sensitive or potentially privileged documents (e.g., joint defense agreements, indemnity agreements, counsel identification for related litigation, participants in petition preparation, funding sources) in every case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many cases do not involve RPI/privity disputes and such documents may be privileged and burdensome to produce, the Office prefers to consider the need for these documents only when a timely, fact-dependent RPI/privity challenge is raised and will evaluate additional discovery on a case-by-case basis under statutory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of discovery in AIA proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in AIA proceedings is significantly more limited than under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure; the statute provides only limited discovery in trial proceedings before the Office (see 35 U.S.C. 316(a)(5), 326(a)(5); 37 CFR 42.51(b)(2), 42.224).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under current practice, discovery requests directed to RPI/privity information are frequently granted only when requests are specific, narrowly tailored, and not unduly burdensome. The Office frequently grants discovery where it satisfies statutory standards and is supported by particular facts in the proceeding; parties may also agree to additional discovery between themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPI/privity determinations are highly fact-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an entity is a real party-in-interest or privy is a highly fact-dependent question not amenable to any bright-line test; the inquiry takes into account how courts have used the terms to justify applying principles of estoppel and preclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and parties should consult common law principles, Federal case law, the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide, and recent Board decisions for guidance; the Office plans further discussion in its Practice Guide and will rely on case law to develop the relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of RPI/privity inquiry (post-filing evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a real party-in-interest or privity is not limited to facts existing at the time of petition filing; supporting evidence that comes into existence after filing may be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bright-line rules limiting inquiry to the filing date would undercut functions like resolving conflicts of interest and applying estoppel; the Office will consider post-filing evidence (e.g., payments made after services rendered) where relevant, as illustrated by Board decisions (e.g., GEA Process Eng’g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of RPI identification and effect on filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must identify all real parties-in-interest per statute (35 U.S.C. 312(a)); if a failure to identify RPI was a mere clerical error, the petitioner may correct the petition without affecting the filing date (see 37 CFR 42.104(c)); other corrections generally require changing the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clerical corrections (limited circumstances) permitted without altering filing date; broader corrections cannot be permitted without affecting filing date because of the statutory requirement to identify all RPIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on standing/RPI lies with petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate burden of proof on the issue of standing and identification of real parties-in-interest lies with the petitioner, who is more likely to possess or have access to evidence relevant to the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patent owner raises sufficient concerns regarding RPI identification, additional discovery may be authorized. Recent Board decisions recognize that the petitioner bears both the burden of producing evidence of standing and the burden of persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties encouraged to confer early on discovery for RPI/privity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office encourages the parties to confer early in the proceeding on additional discovery issues and attempt to reach agreement on a reasonable amount of information to exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early conferral can resolve issues promptly and efficiently; parties may agree to additional discovery per 37 CFR 42.51(b)(2). The Office may consider such agreements when deciding discovery motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion to manage multiple proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has broad discretion to stay, transfer, consolidate, or terminate multiple proceedings (e.g., multiple AIA trials, reexaminations, reissue) involving the same patent claims and will tailor solutions to the unique circumstances of each case to optimize efficiencies and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considers interests of justice and fairness, case-specific facts, and its ability to meet statutory deadlines when managing multiple proceedings; the Office will continue to develop its approach via case law and add discussion to its Practice Guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering the timing of the patent owner’s preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing of the patent owner's preliminary response may be altered when helpful and fair in an appropriate case; no rule change is required to permit such adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may change the preliminary response deadline to manage multiple proceedings or promote efficiency, consistent with fairness and statutory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-identification of repetitive petitions not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners are not required by rule to self-identify that a petition repeats or is substantially similar to previous petitions; petitioners are required, however, to identify other proceedings involving the same challenged patent (37 CFR 42.8(b)(2)) and are encouraged to identify substantive similarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board is positioned to determine whether a later petition raises the same or substantially the same challenges as an earlier petition and will consider whether a later petitioner is amenable to joinder as one relevant factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when deciding to stay, transfer, consolidate, or terminate additional proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant interests include the impact on scheduling and the Office’s ability to meet statutory deadlines, prejudice to the patent owner, and prejudice to the petitioner; these issues are highly fact-specific and the Office requires broad discretion to tailor results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office prefers to allow factors to evolve tethered to the facts of individual cases via case law rather than promulgating a fixed rule divorced from particular facts; the Office will add further discussion to its Practice Guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to stay a copending reexamination or reissue in favor of an AIA trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to stay a copending reexamination or reissue in favor of an AIA trial is determined on a case-by-case basis with factors including overlap of issues, stage of copending proceeding, potential duplication of work, timing relative to the trial, and whether claim amendments are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office has granted and denied stays depending on circumstances (e.g., degree of overlap, stage of reexamination, differences in evidence). The Office will continue case-by-case decisions and will not adopt blanket rule changes at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying Board claim construction to copending reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reexamination is not stayed, questions arise whether the Board’s claim construction should be applied in the reexamination or whether briefing should be allowed; the Office will consider such matters case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No general rule is provided; parties have proposed applying Board constructions to avoid inconsistent decisions, but the Office leaves these determinations to case-specific resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to stay an AIA trial in favor of a copending reexamination/reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA trials are generally not stayed in favor of copending reexamination or reissue because statutory deadlines apply to trials; limited circumstances (e.g., issuance of a new claim in reexamination, late-stage reexamination with significant overlap, agreement of parties) may warrant a stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AIA trials have statutory deadlines and reexaminations/reissues do not, stays of trials are disfavored and will be granted only when warranted by the particular facts; the Office will decide motions to stay on the facts and circumstances of each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of copending reexamination/reissue with an AIA trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidation of an AIA trial with a copending reexamination or reissue is evaluated case-by-case; some commenters find consolidation impractical or prejudicial, while others propose a set of factors to weigh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: type of additional proceeding; time between filings; stage and duration of proceedings; scope and overlap of claims; identity and relations of third-party filers; number of proceedings; whether ex parte reexamination would lose procedures if transferred; relation to district court litigation; appeals; parties' expressed interests; potential cost/resource savings; and ability of the Board to reach timely conclusions. The Office will weigh these and other facts in deciding consolidation.
